claim: Neurons in the hippocampus and adjacent brain areas show a large diversity in their tuning to location and head direction.
source: Neurons in the hippocampus and adjacent brain areas show a large diversity in their tuning to location and head direction, and the underlying circuit mechanisms are not yet resolved.
evidence: This is a general statement about observed neural properties in the hippocampus and adjacent areas, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The underlying circuit mechanisms for spatial tuning diversity are not yet resolved.
source: Neurons in the hippocampus and adjacent brain areas show a large diversity in their tuning to location and head direction, and the underlying circuit mechanisms are not yet resolved.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: It is unclear why certain cell types are selective to one spatial variable but invariant to another.
source: In particular, it is unclear why certain cell types are selective to one spatial variable, but invariant to another.
evidence: This identifies a specific open question in the field.

claim: Place cells are typically invariant to head direction.
source: For example, place cells are typically invariant to head direction.
evidence: This is an established observation about place cell properties.

claim: All observed spatial tuning patterns arise from the same mechanism: excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity driven by the spatial tuning statistics of synaptic inputs.
source: We propose that all observed spatial tuning patterns – in both their selectivity and their invariance – arise from the same mechanism: Excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity driven by the spatial tuning statistics of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Combined excitatory and inhibitory plasticity can lead to localized, grid-like or invariant activity.
source: Using simulations and a mathematical analysis, we show that combined excitatory and inhibitory plasticity can lead to localized, grid-like or invariant activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulations and mathematical analysis presented in the paper.

claim: Combinations of different input statistics along different spatial dimensions reproduce all major spatial tuning patterns observed in rodents.
source: Combinations of different input statistics along different spatial dimensions reproduce all major spatial tuning patterns observed in rodents.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown throughout the paper.

claim: The proposed model is robust to changes in parameters.
source: Our proposed model is robust to changes in parameters, develops patterns on behavioral timescales and makes distinctive experimental predictions.
evidence: This is supported by various simulations with different parameters shown in the paper.

claim: The proposed model develops patterns on behavioral timescales.
source: Our proposed model is robust to changes in parameters, develops patterns on behavioral timescales and makes distinctive experimental predictions.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing pattern emergence within minutes to hours.

claim: Place cells exhibit bell-shaped tuning curves to position.
source: Common observations in these spatial dimensions are localized, bell-shaped tuning curves (O'Keefe, 1976; Taube et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Head direction cells exhibit bell-shaped tuning curves to head direction.
source: Common observations in these spatial dimensions are localized, bell-shaped tuning curves (O'Keefe, 1976; Taube et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Grid cells exhibit periodically repeating activity.
source: periodically repeating activity (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Head direction cells are often invariant to location.
source: For example, head direction cells are often invariant to location (Burgess et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Place cells are commonly invariant to head direction.
source: and place cells are commonly invariant to head direction (Muller et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Several computational models have been suggested to explain the emergence of grid cells.
source: Several computational models have been suggested to explain the emergence of grid cells (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Franzius et al., 2007a; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013; Burgess et al., 2007; Kropff and Treves, 2008; Bush and Burgess, 2014; Castro and Aguiar, 2014; Dordek et al., 2016; Stepanyuk, 2015; Giocomo et al., 2011; Zilli, 2012; D'Albis and Kempter, 2017; Monsalve-Mercado and Leibold, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Most existing models are designed to explain the spatial selectivity of one particular cell type and do not consider invariances along other dimensions.
source: Most of these models are designed to explain the spatial selectivity of one particular cell type and do not consider invariances along other dimensions, although the formation of invariant representations is a non-trivial problem (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the cited literature and knowledge of the field.

claim: The formation of invariant representations is a non-trivial problem.
source: although the formation of invariant representations is a non-trivial problem (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Both observed spatial selectivities and invariances can be explained by a common mechanism of interacting excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity.
source: In this paper we suggest that both the observed spatial selectivities and invariances can be explained by a common mechanism – interacting excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity
evidence: This is the central hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Differences in response profiles of grid, place and head direction cells result from differences in the spatial tuning of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic afferents.
source: and that the observed differences in the response profiles of grid, place and head direction cells result from differences in the spatial tuning of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic afferents.
evidence: This is a key prediction of the proposed model.

claim: The model reproduces the large variety of response patterns of neurons in the hippocampal formation and adjacent areas.
source: Simulations as well as a mathematical analysis indicate that the model reproduces the large variety of response patterns of neurons in the hippocampal formation and adjacent areas
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results and mathematical analysis presented throughout the paper.

claim: The model can be used to make predictions for the input statistics of each cell type.
source: and can be used to make predictions for the input statistics of each cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model's structure and results.

claim: A single model neuron receives feedforward input from excitatory and inhibitory synaptic afferents.
source: A single model neuron that represents a cell in the hippocampal formation or adjacent areas receives feedforward input from excitatory and inhibitory synaptic afferents.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the computational model.

claim: Synaptic afferents are weakly modulated by spatial location.
source: As a simulated rat moves through an environment, these synaptic afferents are weakly modulated by spatial location and in later sections also by head direction.
evidence: This describes the input properties in the model.

claim: The modulation of synaptic afferents is irregular and non-localized with multiple maxima.
source: This modulation is irregular and non-localized with multiple maxima (Buetfering et al., 2014); see Figure 1a and Materials and methods.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Different inputs show different modulation profiles and each profile is temporally stable.
source: Importantly, different inputs show different modulation profiles and each profile is temporally stable.
evidence: This describes a key property of the model inputs.

claim: The output rate is given by a weighted sum of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: The output rate is given by a weighted sum of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This describes the model's output computation.

claim: Excitatory weights change according to a Hebbian plasticity rule.
source: In our model, both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic weights are subject to plasticity. The excitatory weights change according to a Hebbian plasticity rule (Hebb, 1949) that potentiates the weights in response to simultaneous pre- and postsynaptic activity.
evidence: This describes the excitatory plasticity rule used in the model, with citation to Hebb.

claim: Inhibitory synapses evolve according to a plasticity rule that changes their weights in proportion to presynaptic activity and the difference between postsynaptic activity and a target rate.
source: The inhibitory synapses evolve according to a plasticity rule that changes their weights in proportion to presynaptic activity and the difference between postsynaptic activity and a target rate (1 Hz in all simulations).
evidence: This describes the inhibitory plasticity rule used in the model.

claim: The inhibitory plasticity rule has previously been shown to balance excitation and inhibition such that the firing rate of the output neuron approaches the target rate.
source: This rule has previously been shown to balance excitation and inhibition such that the firing rate of the output neuron approaches the target rate (Vogels et al., 2011; D'Amour and Froemke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity acts fast enough to track changes of excitatory weights, so that excitation and inhibition are approximately balanced at all times.
source: We assume the inhibitory plasticity will act fast enough to track changes of excitatory weights, so that excitation and inhibition are approximately balanced at all times.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the model.

claim: If the inhibitory tuning is smoother than the excitatory tuning, the output neuron develops equidistant firing fields, reminiscent of grid cells on a linear track.
source: If the inhibitory tuning is smoother than the excitatory tuning (Figure 1b), the output neuron develops equidistant firing fields, reminiscent of grid cells on a linear track (Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1b and supported by citation.

claim: If the excitatory tuning is smoother than the inhibitory tuning, the output neuron fires close to the target rate of 1 Hz everywhere, developing a spatial invariance.
source: If instead the excitatory tuning is smoother, the output neuron fires close to the target rate of 1 Hz everywhere (Figure 1c); it develops a spatial invariance.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1c.

claim: For spatially untuned inhibitory afferents, the output neuron develops a single firing field, reminiscent of a one-dimensional place cell.
source: For spatially untuned inhibitory afferents (Grienberger et al., 2017), the output neuron develops a single firing field, reminiscent of a one-dimensional place cell (Figure 1d); (cf. Clopath et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1d and supported by citations.

claim: A small potentiation of one excitatory weight leads to an increased firing rate of the output neuron at the location of the associated place field.
source: From this homogeneous state, a small potentiation of one excitatory weight leads to an increased firing rate of the output neuron at the location of the associated place field (highlighted red curve in Figure 1e).
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: The inhibitory learning rule increases the synaptic weight of inhibitory inputs that are tuned to the same location to bring the output neuron back to the target rate.
source: To bring the output neuron back to the target rate, the inhibitory learning rule increases the synaptic weight of inhibitory inputs that are tuned to the same location (highlighted blue curve in Figure 1e).
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: If inhibitory inputs have smaller place fields than excitatory inputs, inhibitory plasticity can stabilize spatial invariance.
source: If these inhibitory inputs have smaller place fields than the excitatory inputs (Figure 1c), this restores the target rate everywhere (Vogels et al., 2011). Hence, inhibitory plasticity can stabilize spatial invariance if the inhibitory inputs are sufficiently precise (i.e. not too smooth) in space.
evidence: This is explained in the text with reference to Figure 1c and supported by citation.

claim: If the spatial tuning of inhibitory inputs is smoother than that of excitatory inputs, the target firing rate cannot be restored everywhere.
source: In contrast, if the spatial tuning of the inhibitory inputs is smoother than that of the excitatory inputs, the target firing rate cannot be restored everywhere.
evidence: This is explained as part of the mechanism description.

claim: The compensatory potentiation of inhibitory weights leads to a corona of inhibition, in which the output neuron cannot fire.
source: Instead, the compensatory potentiation of inhibitory weights increases the inhibition in a spatial region at least the size of the inhibitory place fields. This leads to a corona of inhibition, in which the output neuron cannot fire (Figure 1e, blue region).
evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: Outside of the inhibitory surround the output neuron can fire again and the next firing field develops.
source: Outside of this inhibitory surround the output neuron can fire again and the next firing field develops.
evidence: This is explained as part of the mechanism description.

claim: Iterated, the mechanism results in a periodic arrangement of firing fields.
source: Iterated, this results in a periodic arrangement of firing fields (Figure 1f and Figure 7b for a depiction of the input currents).
evidence: This is explained in the text and demonstrated in Figures 1f and 7b.

claim: Spatially untuned inhibition corresponds to a large inhibitory corona that exceeds the length of the linear track, so that only a single place field remains.
source: Spatially untuned inhibition corresponds to a large inhibitory corona that exceeds the length of the linear track, so that only a single place field remains.
evidence: This is explained as part of the mechanism description.

claim: The width of individual firing fields is determined by the smoothness of the excitatory input tuning.
source: The above reasoning suggests that the width of individual firing fields is determined by the smoothness of the excitatory input tuning
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism description.

claim: The distance between grid fields (grid spacing) is set by the smoothness of the inhibitory input tuning.
source: while the distance between grid fields, that is, the grid spacing, is set by the smoothness of the inhibitory input tuning.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism description.

claim: The grid spacing scales linearly with the inhibitory smoothness in a large range, both for localized and non-localized input tuning.
source: Indeed, both simulations and a mathematical analysis (Materials and methods) confirm that the grid spacing scales linearly with the inhibitory smoothness in a large range, both for localized (Figure 1g) and non-localized input tuning (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figures 1g and 1h and mathematical analysis.

claim: The grid spacing has a weak logarithmic dependence on the ratio of the learning rates, the mean firing rates and the number of afferents of the excitatory and inhibitory population.
source: The analysis also reveals a weak logarithmic dependence of the grid spacing on the ratio of the learning rates, the mean firing rates and the number of afferents of the excitatory and inhibitory population (Equation 78 and Figure 8b).
evidence: This is revealed by the mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The interaction of excitatory and inhibitory plasticity can lead to spatial invariance, spatially periodic activity patterns or single place fields depending on the spatial statistics of the excitatory and inhibitory input.
source: In summary, the interaction of excitatory and inhibitory plasticity can lead to spatial invariance, spatially periodic activity patterns or single place fields depending on the spatial statistics of the excitatory and inhibitory input.
evidence: This summarizes the main findings from the linear track simulations.

claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex show pronounced hexagonal symmetry when a rat navigates in a two-dimensional arena.
source: When a rat navigates in a two-dimensional arena, the spatial firing maps of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) show pronounced hexagonal symmetry (Hafting et al., 2005; Fyhn et al., 2004) with different grid spacings and spatial phases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The rat explores the arena for 10 hr, following trajectories extracted from behavioral data.
source: The rat explores the arena for 10 hr, following trajectories extracted from behavioral data (Sargolini et al., 2006b); Materials and methods.
evidence: This describes the simulation setup.

claim: Before learning, the spatial tuning of the output neuron shows no symmetry.
source: Before learning, the spatial tuning of the output neuron shows no symmetry.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a,b,c.

claim: After 10 hr of spatial exploration, the output neuron developed a hexagonal pattern for all three input classes.
source: While the rat forages through the environment, the output cell develops a periodic firing pattern for all three input classes, reminiscent of grid cells in the mEC (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) and typically with the same hexagonal symmetry.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2a,b,c and supported by citations.

claim: The hexagonal arrangement results from smoother inhibitory input tuning, which generates a spherical inhibitory corona around each firing field.
source: This hexagonal arrangement is again a result of smoother inhibitory input tuning, which generates a spherical inhibitory corona around each firing field (compare Figure 1e).
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism and compared to Figure 1e.

claim: Center-surround fields are arranged in a hexagonal pattern, which is the closest packing of spheres in two dimensions.
source: These center-surround fields are arranged in a hexagonal pattern – the closest packing of spheres in two dimensions; (cf. Turing, 1952).
evidence: This is based on geometric principles and supported by citation to Turing.

claim: The spacing of the hexagonal pattern is determined by the inhibitory smoothness.
source: We find that the spacing of this pattern is determined by the inhibitory smoothness.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations and analysis.

claim: The similarity between cells in terms of orientation and phase of the grid depends on whether they receive the same inputs, on the trajectories on which the tuning was learned and on the initial synaptic weights.
source: The similarity between cells in terms of orientation and phase of the grid depends – in decreasing order – on whether they receive the same inputs, on the trajectories on which the tuning was learned and on the initial synaptic weights (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two grid cells can have different phase and orientation, even if they share a large fraction or all of their inputs.
source: Two grid cells can thus have different phase and orientation, even if they share a large fraction or all of their inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: For place cell-like input, most of the output cells develop a positive grid score during 10 hr of spatial exploration (33% before to 86% after learning).
source: For place cell-like input, most of the output cells develop a positive grid score during 10 hr of spatial exploration (33% before to 86% after learning, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Even for low grid scores, the firing rate maps look grid-like after learning but exhibit a distorted symmetry.
source: Even for low grid scores, the firing rate maps look grid-like after learning but exhibit a distorted symmetry (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d.

claim: For sparse non-localized input, the fraction of output cells with a positive grid score increases from 35% to 87% within 10 hr of spatial exploration.
source: For sparse non-localized input, the fraction of output cells with a positive grid score increases from 35% to 87%
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2e.

claim: For dense non-localized input, the fraction of output cells with a positive grid score increases from 16% to 68% within 10 hr of spatial exploration.
source: and for dense non-localized input from 16% to 68% within 10 hr of spatial exploration (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The excitatory and inhibitory inputs are not required to have the same tuning statistics.
source: The excitatory and inhibitory inputs are not required to have the same tuning statistics.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Grid patterns also emerge when excitation is localized and inhibition is non-localized.
source: Grid patterns also emerge when excitation is localized and inhibition is non-localized (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The interaction of excitatory and inhibitory plasticity leads to grid-like firing patterns in the output neuron for all three input scenarios.
source: In summary, the interaction of excitatory and inhibitory plasticity leads to grid-like firing patterns in the output neuron for all three input scenarios.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the 2D simulations.

claim: The grids are typically less distorted for sparser input.
source: The grids are typically less distorted for sparser input (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2g.

claim: In unfamiliar environments, neurons in the mEC exhibit grid-like firing patterns within minutes.
source: In unfamiliar environments, neurons in the mEC exhibit grid-like firing patterns within minutes (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Grid cells react quickly to changes in the environment.
source: Moreover, grid cells react quickly to changes in the environment (Fyhn et al., 2007; Savelli et al., 2008; Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: For place cell-like input, periodic patterns can be discerned within 10 min of spatial exploration, starting with random initial weights.
source: For place cell-like input, periodic patterns can be discerned within 10 min of spatial exploration, starting with random initial weights (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The pattern further emphasizes over time and remains stable for many hours.
source: The pattern further emphasizes over time and remains stable for many hours (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In 500 realizations with different trajectories, initial synaptic weights and locations of input place fields, a periodic pattern emerged within the first 30 min in all simulations.
source: To investigate the robustness of this phenomenon, we ran 500 realizations with different trajectories, initial synaptic weights and locations of input place fields. In all simulations, a periodic pattern emerged within the first 30 min
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A majority of patterns exhibited hexagonal symmetry after 3 hr (increasing from 33% to 81%).
source: and a majority of patterns exhibited hexagonal symmetry after 3 hr (increasing from 33% to 81%, Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: For non-localized input, the emergence of the final grids typically takes longer, but the first grid fields are also observed within minutes.
source: For non-localized input, the emergence of the final grids typically takes longer, but the first grid fields are also observed within minutes and are still present in the final grid, as observed in experiments (Hafting et al., 2005); (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and supported by citation.

claim: The output firing pattern is robust to perturbations, even if more than half of the inputs are remapped.
source: We find that the output firing pattern is robust to such perturbations, even if more than half of the inputs are remapped (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: If all inputs are changed, corresponding to a novel room, a grid pattern is learned anew.
source: If all inputs are changed, corresponding to a novel room, a grid pattern is learned anew.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strong initial pattern in the weights does not hinder the development of a new grid pattern.
source: The strong initial pattern in the weights does not hinder this development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In an arena separated by a wall, single grid cells form two independent grid patterns — one on each side of the wall — that coalesce once the wall is removed.
source: Recently, Wernle et al., 2018 discovered that in an arena separated by a wall, single grid cells form two independent grid patterns — one on each side of the wall — that coalesce once the wall is removed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wernle et al., 2018.

claim: Grid fields close to the partition wall move to establish a more coherent pattern, while fields far away from the partition wall do not change their locations.
source: They find that grid fields close to the partition wall move to establish a more coherent pattern. In contrast, fields far away from the partition wall do not change their locations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wernle et al., 2018.

claim: As observed experimentally, grid fields close to the former partition line rearrange to make the two grids more coherent and grid fields far away from the partition line basically stay where they were.
source: As observed experimentally, grid fields close to the former partition line rearrange to make the two grids more coherent and grid fields far away from the partition line basically stay where they were (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4d.

claim: Periodic patterns emerge rapidly in the model and the associated time scale is limited primarily by how quickly the animal visits its surroundings.
source: In summary, periodic patterns emerge rapidly in our model and the associated time scale is limited primarily by how quickly the animal visits its surroundings, that is, by the same time scale that limits the experimental recognition of the grids.
evidence: This summarizes the findings on rapid pattern emergence.

claim: Place cells emerge from a very smooth inhibitory input tuning in a two-dimensional arena.
source: We first verified that also in a two-dimensional arena, place cells emerge from a very smooth inhibitory input tuning (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5a,b.

claim: The emergence of place cells is independent of the exact shape of the excitatory input.
source: The emergence of place cells is independent of the exact shape of the excitatory input.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: Non-localized inputs lead to similar results as those from grid cell-like inputs of different orientation and grid spacing.
source: Non-localized inputs (Figure 5a) lead to similar results as those from grid cell-like inputs of different orientation and grid spacing (Figure 5b, Methods and materials)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Spatial invariance results when excitation is broader than inhibition in two dimensions.
source: Next we verified that also in two dimensions, spatial invariance results when excitation is broader than inhibition (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5c.

claim: If the spatial tuning of inhibitory inputs is smoother than the tuning of the excitatory inputs along one dimension but less smooth along the other, the output neuron develops band cell-like firing patterns.
source: We then varied the smoothness of the inhibitory inputs independently along two spatial directions. If the spatial tuning of inhibitory inputs is smoother than the tuning of the excitatory inputs along one dimension but less smooth along the other, the output neuron develops band cell-like firing patterns (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5d.

claim: If inhibitory input is smoother than excitatory input, but not isotropic, the output cell develops stretched grids with different spacing along two axes.
source: If inhibitory input is smoother than excitatory input, but not isotropic, the output cell develops stretched grids with different spacing along two axes (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5e.

claim: For anisotropic cases, stretched hexagonal grids and rectangular arrangements of firing fields appear similarly favorable.
source: For these anisotropic cases, stretched hexagonal grids and rectangular arrangements of firing fields appear similarly favorable (compare Figure 5e, second row and column).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5e.

claim: A hexagonal arrangement is favored by a dense packing of inhibitory coronas, whereas a rectangular arrangement would maximize the proximity of the excitatory centers.
source: A hexagonal arrangement is favored by a dense packing of inhibitory coronas, whereas a rectangular arrangement would maximize the proximity of the excitatory centers, given the inhibitory corona (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explained in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relative spatial smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory input determines the symmetry of the spatial firing pattern of the output neuron.
source: In summary, the relative spatial smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory input determines the symmetry of the spatial firing pattern of the output neuron.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the simulations with different input statistics.

claim: The requirements for the input tuning that support invariance, periodicity and localization apply individually to each spatial dimension, opening up a combinatorial variety of spatial tuning patterns.
source: The requirements for the input tuning that support invariance, periodicity and localization apply individually to each spatial dimension, opening up a combinatorial variety of spatial tuning patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Many cells in and around the hippocampus are tuned to the head direction of the animal.
source: Many cells in and around the hippocampus are tuned to the head direction of the animal (Taube et al., 1990; Taube, 1995; Chen et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Head direction cells are typically tuned to a single head direction, just like place cells are typically tuned to a single location.
source: These head direction cells are typically tuned to a single head direction, just like place cells are typically tuned to a single location.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Conjunctive cells in the mEC fire like grid cells in space, but only in a particular head direction.
source: Conjunctive cells in the mEC fire like grid cells in space, but only in a particular head direction (Sargolini et al., 2006a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Many place cells in the hippocampus of crawling bats also exhibit head direction tuning.
source: and many place cells in the hippocampus of crawling bats also exhibit head direction tuning (Rubin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The spatial tuning of the output neuron is determined by the relative spatial smoothness of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: In line with the previous observations, we find that the spatial tuning of the output neuron is determined by the relative spatial smoothness of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: The head direction tuning of the output neuron is determined by the relative smoothness of the head direction tuning of the inputs from the two populations.
source: and the head direction tuning of the output neuron is determined by the relative smoothness of the head direction tuning of the inputs from the two populations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: If the head direction tuning of excitatory input neurons is smoother than that of inhibitory input neurons, the output neuron becomes invariant to head direction.
source: If the head direction tuning of excitatory input neurons is smoother than that of inhibitory input neurons, the output neuron becomes invariant to head direction (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6a.

claim: If instead only the excitatory input is tuned to head direction, the output neuron develops a single activity bump at a particular head direction.
source: If instead only the excitatory input is tuned to head direction, the output neuron develops a single activity bump at a particular head direction (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6b,c.

claim: For spatially smooth inhibitory input, the output neuron develops a hexagonal firing pattern.
source: The concurrent spatial tuning of the inhibitory input neurons determines the spatial tuning of the output neuron. For spatially smooth inhibitory input, the output neuron develops a hexagonal firing pattern (Figure 6a,b)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6a,b.

claim: For less smooth inhibitory input the firing of the output neuron is invariant to the location of the animal.
source: and for less smooth inhibitory input the firing of the output neuron is invariant to the location of the animal (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6c.

claim: The relative smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory input neurons in space and in head direction determines whether the output cell fires like a pure grid cell, a conjunctive cell or a pure head direction cell.
source: In summary, the relative smoothness of inhibitory and excitatory input neurons in space and in head direction determines whether the output cell fires like a pure grid cell, a conjunctive cell or a pure head direction cell (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6d.

claim: The overall head direction tuning of conjunctive cells is broader than that of individual grid fields.
source: We find that the overall head direction tuning of conjunctive cells is broader than that of individual grid fields (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6e.

claim: The broader overall head direction tuning results from variations in the preferred head direction of different grid fields.
source: This results from variations in the preferred head direction of different grid fields.
evidence: This is inferred from Figure 6e.

claim: Individual grid fields tend to align their head direction tuning.
source: Typically, however, these variations remain small enough to preserve an overall head direction tuning of the cell, because individual grid fields tend to align their head direction tuning (compare with Figure 5—figure supplement 1, but in three dimensions).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations.

claim: The main prediction of the model is that the spatial autocorrelation structure of excitatory and inhibitory inputs determines – and should thus be predictable from – the output pattern of the cell.
source: The main prediction of the model is that the spatial autocorrelation structure of excitatory and inhibitory inputs determines – and should thus be predictable from – the output pattern of the cell.
evidence: This is the key experimental prediction of the model.

claim: Investigations of the tuning of individual cells or even synapses that project to spatially tuned cells would be a litmus test for the proposed mechanism.
source: Investigations of the tuning of individual cells (Wertz et al., 2015) or even synapses (Wilson et al., 2016) that project to spatially tuned cells would thus be a litmus test for the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental test with citations to relevant techniques.

claim: The origin of synaptic input to spatially tuned cells is not fully resolved.
source: The origin of synaptic input to spatially tuned cells is not fully resolved (van Strien et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The model is consistent with input from higher sensory areas that could inherit spatial tuning from their sensory tuning in a stable environment.
source: Given that our model is robust to the precise properties of the input, it is consistent with input from higher sensory areas (Tanaka, 1996; Quiroga et al., 2005) that could inherit spatial tuning from their sensory tuning in a stable environment (Arleo and Gerstner, 2000; Franzius et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a speculation about input sources.

claim: Grid cells lose their firing profiles in darkness.
source: This is in line with the observation that grid cells lose their firing profiles in darkness (Chen et al., 2016; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The hexagonal pattern of grid cells rotates when a visual cue card is rotated.
